newsitem.title: USA: Clinton begins debate prep "slightly apprehensive". [CORRECTED 00:27 GMT 4/10]
newsitem.headline: Clinton begins debate prep "slightly apprehensive". [CORRECTED 00:27 GMT 4/10]

text.p: Returning to the political ring after an inconclusive flurry of Middle East diplomacy, a "slightly apprehensive" President Bill Clinton started training on Thursday for his first campaign debate with Republican rival Bob Dole.

Clinton, accompanied by a coterie of aides not unlike a prizefighter's team of handlers, settled in at the Athenaeum Hotel, a 105-year-old mansion on the grounds of the Chautauqua Institution, for three days of cramming for his clash with Dole in Hartford, Connecticut, on Sunday night.

Campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart told reporters that Clinton, who is famed for his speaking skills, was "slightly apprehensive at this point" because Dole has been prepping for the debate while Clinton was trying to end the violence between Israelis and Palestinians that erupted last week.

White House press secretary Mike McCurry also tried to lower expectations for what most experts believe will be a stellar presidential performance, saying Clinton "feels like he has not had the time he had allotted and planned to prepare for the debates."

Aides said Clinton's preparations for his showdown with Dole would include a series of mock debates in which former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell will impersonate the Republican challenger.
The dress rehearsals were to take place each evening to let Clinton adjust his body clock for the real thing.

Clinton's debate coaches included Democratic consultant Mike Sheehan, a graduate of the Yale Drama School and Washington's Folger Shakespeare Theatre. Aides said Clinton would also study briefing books and spend some time relaxing, perhaps with jogging and golf.

During a brief stop in Buffalo on his way to this gated Victorian village that has long been a magnet for intellectuals, Clinton previewed themes he was expected to emphasise in Sunday night's debate.

He told cheering supporters at an airport pep rally that when he ran for president in 1992 "we were drifting toward the 21st Century" and "four years later, we're on the right track roaring toward the 21st Century."

"Compared to four years ago, there's a lot of good news. Ten and a half million new jobs. Average family income is up $1,600 after inflation since we passed the economic plan that our opponents said would drive the country into the ditch," he said.

Clinton was, in a sense, encroaching on enemy turf by choosing western New York for his debate training camp. Jack Kemp, Dole's vice-presidential running mate, represented the Buffalo area in Congress for more than a decade.
The Chautauqua institution is located 60 miles (96 km) southwest of Buffalo on a wooded 750-acre (303 hectare) campus overlooking a lake.

Saluting high school bands who turned out to greet him, Clinton joked about the frigid weather the region is famous for -- it was in the low 40s (about five degrees Celsius) for his arrival. "The colder it is, the harder it is to play one of those instruments -- I know," the former saxaphone player said.
"But in Buffalo, this is a heat wave, right?" Clinton said.

Clinton mentioned his emergency summit with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (corrects from Yitzhak Rabin), Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and King Hussein of Jordan only in passing. But White House spokesman Mike McCurry rejected Republican criticism of the summit's failure to produce concrete results.
McCurry defied Dole and Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich to identify "any other course of action than the president saw" for preventing collapse of the Middle East peace process.
Sunday's debate between Clinton and Dole will be followed by a vice presidential showdown between Kemp and Al Gore on Wednesday night, and a second Clinton-Dole debate on Wednesday, Oct. 16.

Clinton enters the rhetorical fray in a strong position politically. With less than five weeks to go before the Nov. 5 election, he leads his rival by 10 to 15 percentage points or more in national opinion polls.
